conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - September 3, 2025
conflicts.issue: New UDO Affordable Housing Density Bonus Design (Deep 30% AMI Subsidies vs. Broader 70%-80% AMI By-Right Bonuses)
conflicts.summary: JCCPC members debated how the New UDO's affordable housing density bonus should balance modest by-right incentives at 70%-80% AMI against deeper affordability targets at 30% AMI that typically require direct public subsidy.
conflicts.side_a_position: Focus zoning bonuses on feasible market-driven thresholds (e.g., 60%-80% AMI or Austin-style 100% affordable by-right deregulation) paired with fee-in-lieu flexibility.
side_a_arguments: By-right zoning bonuses cannot mathematically cross-subsidize 30% AMI units without LIHTC or local bond dollars, so overly steep rules go unused.
Austin's 'Affordability Unlocked' model proves stripping height, parking, and setback barriers unlocks significantly more subsidized supply.
conflicts.side_b_position: Guard against eroding resident leverage and ensure density bonuses deliver meaningful deeply affordable units and neighborhood benefits.
side_b_arguments: Durham's greatest unmet shortage is for households at 30%-50% AMI, which developers routinely skip when bonuses stop at 80% AMI.
Giving away extra height and density by-right without calibrated requirements risks upzoning land values without proportionate community benefit.
conflicts.resolution: Informational workshop only; consultants and planning staff recorded committee feedback to calibrate draft UDO housing incentives.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) December 3, 2025
conflicts.issue: New UDO Minimum Acreage Threshold for Planned Development Districts
conflicts.summary: Committee members disagreed on staff's proposed 150-acre minimum site size to qualify for a Planned Development (PD) zoning district.
conflicts.side_a_position: Lower the Planned Development threshold to 50–80 acres to encourage cohesive master-planned infill inside the Urban Growth Boundary.
side_a_arguments: Few contiguous parcels inside the Urban Growth Boundary reach 150 acres, so a high floor effectively restricts Planned Developments to greenfield sprawl.
Medium-scale 50–80 acre sites can coordinate streets, parks, and mixed uses without relying on ad-hoc rezonings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain a higher threshold (~100–150 acres) so Planned Development entitlements are tied to major infrastructure and community benefits.
side_b_arguments: Smaller projects rarely have the financial capacity to deliver schools, regional parks, or transformative community benefits.
A ~100-acre compromise avoids opening PD flexibility to mid-sized sites lacking meaningful public-benefit leverage.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to study a smaller PD threshold option and return with refined analysis in January 2026.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - August 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: New UDO Broad By-Right Upzoning vs. Preserving Base Zoning Leverage for Affordable Housing Density Bonuses
conflicts.summary: Committee members clashed over staff's draft UDO zoning capacity analysis, which increases by-right residential capacity inside the Urban Growth Boundary by 46% from 136,445 to 200,072 units.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold base by-right zoning closer to current capacity and tie significant additional height/density to calibrated affordable housing and green-building density bonuses.
side_a_arguments: Expanding by-right zoning to 200,072+ units gives away valuable development rights for free, especially under North Carolina's recent ban on local downzoning.
Without holding base zoning low enough to require developers to opt in, Durham loses leverage to extract affordable units and green building features via density bonuses.
Extra height (such as increasing 3-story corridors to 10-30 stories) should be unlocked through market-calibrated bonus tiers rather than unconditioned by-right entitlements.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain broad by-right residential upzoning inside the UGB to expand total housing supply, support walkable 15-minute neighborhoods, and rely on direct public subsidies for deep affordability.
side_b_arguments: Durham's existing 15% affordable housing density bonus has historically produced very few units because 0-30% AMI housing requires direct capital subsidies and revolving loan funds rather than zoning trades alone.
Restricting base supply risks Chapel Hill-style exclusionary outcomes—declining school enrollment, soaring home prices, and loss of Black residents.
Recent local market data (12% multifamily vacancy) indicates increased by-right supply helps moderate market rents while containing sprawl within the Urban Growth Boundary.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; committee directed Planning staff to return with data on historical density bonus uptake, Minneapolis inclusionary zoning comparisons, and visual scenario illustrations.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - January 8, 2025
conflicts.issue: TC2400003 Tree Coverage Negotiation Flexibility in Statutory Development Agreements vs. Canopy Equity & UDO Freeze
conflicts.summary: Committee members split over whether to allow developers entering statutory development agreements to negotiate down UDO tree-coverage requirements for affordable housing projects like 160-unit Page Corners.
conflicts.side_a_position: Express strong caution about lowering suburban tree-coverage rules mid-UDO-rewrite given heat-island inequities and potential overuse of waivers.
side_a_arguments: Comprehensive Plan Policies 26, 85, and 94-96 call for equitable tree canopy and reducing urban heat islands and energy bills in lower-income housing.
Members understood the City was pausing ad hoc UDO text amendments during the full UDO rewrite, and Baker wanted assurance site layouts maximize efficiency rather than excessive parking/setbacks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support permitting statutory development agreements to weigh tree-coverage adjustments against major community benefits such as 160 deeply affordable LIHTC apartments.
side_b_arguments: State housing finance agency parking rules (1.5 spaces/unit) and stormwater SCMs leave insufficient space for 20% Suburban tree coverage; local code shouldn't create self-inflicted barriers to $38M in affordable housing.

Because every statutory development agreement requires elected governing-board approval, Council retains full discretion to reject poor tradeoffs while avoiding overly narrow climate metrics that block housing or solar.
conflicts.resolution: Informational review; staff noted the privately initiated amendment cannot be blocked from proceeding through neighborhood meetings, Planning Commission, and Council.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - January 8, 2025
conflicts.issue: Stormwater Exempt-Plat Rules Disincentivizing Triplexes & Quadplexes Under the New UDO
conflicts.summary: While not an explicit member-vs-member split, members and staff highlighted policy tension between UDO infill density goals and separate Public Works stormwater rules that exempt fee-simple single-family/duplex lots while penalizing missing-middle plexes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Coordinate Public Works and County Stormwater reforms alongside the UDO rewrite so compact multi-unit housing (triplexes/quadplexes) is not penalized relative to exempt-plat single-family infill.
side_a_arguments: Separate exempt-plat single-family driveways can generate more untreated impervious surface than a shared triplex/quadplex yet escape costly engineering analyses.
Without parallel stormwater reforms (such as footprint-based thresholds or Hillsboro-style topsoil/compost amendments), New UDO missing-middle zoning will fail to deliver diverse housing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution against altering stormwater thresholds without thorough engineering and state NPDES/EMC compliance review to avoid worsening downstream flooding.
side_b_arguments: Staff noted stormwater rules live outside the UDO and require technical capacity, state approvals, and careful maintenance oversight for green infrastructure like permeable pavement.
conflicts.resolution: Director Sara Young agreed to consult Public Works and County Stormwater leadership (Ryan Eaves) on feasible follow-up recommendations.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) December 3, 2025
conflicts.issue: Pace of New UDO Adoption Timeline vs. Planning Commission Review Depth
conflicts.summary: Javiera Caballero and Nate Baker clashed sharply over community engagement effectiveness (citing Northgate Mall) and whether the New UDO schedule should be accelerated or preserve multi-meeting Planning Commission review.
conflicts.side_a_position: Expedite New UDO adoption and tighten Planning Commission review timelines while reassessing traditional engagement channels.
side_a_arguments: Community engagement around Northgate Mall produced confusion and failed to reflect neighborhood priorities compared to Braggtown outreach.
Delaying UDO adoption slows implementation of Comprehensive Plan housing and equitable growth policies.
conflicts.side_b_position: Preserve thorough Planning Commission deliberation across multiple meetings rather than rushing the UDO rewrite.
side_b_arguments: Planning Commissioners cannot responsibly digest a massive new development code and zoning map in a single rushed session.
North Carolina state restrictions on downzoning make getting the initial UDO mapping right even more consequential.
conflicts.resolution: Staff committed to returning in January 2026 with a revised schedule allocating two earlier Planning Commission meetings ahead of governing-body public hearings.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC)
conflicts.issue: Blanket By-Right Affordable Housing Density Bonuses vs. Discretionary Review and Anti-Displacement Safeguards
conflicts.summary: Javiera Caballero and Nate Baker debated the Durham Housing Initiative Task Force recommendation to expand blanket by-right residential density bonuses across residential zoning districts.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support broader by-right density bonuses tied to affordability commitments and faster approvals to lower housing construction barriers.
side_a_arguments: Discretionary rezoning slows affordable housing production and increases financing uncertainty and legal costs.
Clear by-right rules allow mission-driven and infill builders to add modest multi-unit supply without protracted political hearings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Exercise caution with blanket by-right bonuses and preserve discretionary or context-sensitive checks in vulnerable neighborhoods.
side_b_arguments: Blanket by-right bonuses risk fueling speculative land assembly and displacement in historically underserved neighborhoods.
Community input and discretionary conditions are needed to secure deeper affordability, infrastructure commitments, and neighborhood fit.
conflicts.resolution: Informational task force discussion; no formal vote taken, with policy options carried into ongoing New UDO drafting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC)
conflicts.issue: New UDO Compact Infill Standards, Base Building Heights (3 vs. 5 Stories), and UDO Delivery Timeline
conflicts.summary: Members differed over compact RD2 infill specifications, height caps (3 vs. 5 stories), and how aggressively to pace the New UDO schedule toward June 2026 adoption.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize compact walkable urban form, calibrated RD2 infill, and sustainable development standards even if thorough code refinement takes time.
side_a_arguments: Allowing sprawling suburban patterns or weak design criteria undermines walkability and climate goals.
Height transitions and compact infill blocks must be carefully calibrated in the code rather than leaving loopholes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the UDO adoption schedule on track for June 2026 and establish clear metrics on open-space preservation and attainable housing heights.
side_b_arguments: Allowing slightly taller by-right or bonus heights (up to 5 stories in appropriate corridors) expands affordable and mixed-income capacity.
Governing bodies need verifiable baseline data on Durham's 30% protected open-space target and steady progress toward a June 2026 adoption vote.
conflicts.resolution: Staff confirmed plans to bring draft Plan District standards, zoning maps, and an update on open-space data back to the December JCCPC meeting ahead of a June 2026 adoption target.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) June 4, 2025 - AUDIO DIFFICULTIES
conflicts.issue: New UDO Corridor Height & By-Right Upzoning vs. Density Bonus Leverage
conflicts.summary: Council Members Nate Baker and Javiera Caballero disagreed over whether broad upzoning in the draft UDO map gives away height and density without securing affordable housing and walkability concessions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Preserve lower base heights and require developers to earn extra stories through calibrated density bonuses and the '3Ds' of walkable design.
side_a_arguments: Giving away four or more extra stories by right surrenders public leverage to secure affordable units and community benefits.
Density alone does not produce walkable neighborhoods without diversity and design standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Enact macro-level by-right upzoning across urban corridors to achieve a 15-minute city within the UGB and pair it with direct subsidies for deep affordability.
side_b_arguments: Density bonuses rarely deliver 30-50% AMI housing without direct public subsidy.
Failing to expand by-right housing inside the UGB risks Chapel Hill-style exclusionary housing inflation and displacement.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; discussion carried over to the August 6, 2025 JCCPC meeting alongside staff's zoning capacity modeling.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) May 7, 2025
conflicts.issue: Vision Zero Implementation: Driver Behavior Education vs. Street Design, Quick-Build Delays, and Density Bonuses
conflicts.summary: JCCPC members differed on whether driver education or physical street engineering should carry priority in Vision Zero, while Vice Chair Baker and Mayor Williams challenged staff on right-of-way splits, density bonuses, and quick-build execution speed.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question emphasizing driver behavior/education vs. built environment, or challenge density bonuses and right-of-way allocations that prioritize cars over multimodal street space.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Lee asked why driver education sits higher on the safe-systems pyramid when reckless driving causes crashes.

Nate Baker argued against relying on density bonuses for basic pedestrian safety instead of universal upzoning and urged dedicating at least 50% of right-of-way space to multimodal/pedestrian infrastructure rather than mostly cars.
conflicts.side_b_position: Focus on systemic street engineering, rapid quick-build interventions in Black-majority high-injury corridors, and practical incremental UDO incentives.
side_b_arguments: Lauren Grove explained public-health evidence shows changing roadway geometry and speeds protects everyone regardless of human error.

Leonardo Williams pressed staff for the top 10 dangerous intersections by neighborhood demographics and demanded accelerating physical quick-build barriers rather than waiting years for full rebuilds.
conflicts.resolution: Informational workshop item; staff committed to sharing top-10 intersection racial/demographic data and incorporating committee feedback into UDO Module 2/3 drafts and Multimodal TIA budget requests.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - April 2, 2025
conflicts.issue: Elimination of Minimum Parking Requirements in New UDO Module 2
conflicts.summary: Committee members differed over whether the new UDO should maintain complete elimination of off-street parking minimums in an auto-oriented city or monitor and revisit spillover impacts.
conflicts.side_a_position: Concerned about zero parking minimums causing street spillover and public/visitor parking burdens.
side_a_arguments: Durham remains heavily auto-dependent and visitors still drive to businesses and neighborhoods.
Without minimum parking requirements, private developments may shift parking costs and spillover burdens onto neighboring streets and the public.
conflicts.side_b_position: Strongly support permanently eliminating parking minimums to reduce housing/development costs and public parking debt.
side_b_arguments: Eliminating parking minimums was a hard-fought SCAD/UDO victory aligned with Durham's Comprehensive Plan.
Oversupplying parking created substantial debt and deficits in the City's downtown parking fund for underutilized garages.
conflicts.resolution: Staff confirmed there is no Council/County direction to restore parking minimums and that staff will monitor real-world impacts after adoption.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - April 2, 2025
conflicts.issue: Retaining Versus Eliminating Neighborhood Protection Overlays (NPOs) in New UDO
conflicts.summary: Members debated whether Neighborhood Protection Overlays reinforce inequitable density exclusion or can be reformed with guardrails to discourage small-home teardowns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Oppose retaining NPOs due to redundancy, lack of petition thresholds, and inequitable barriers to citywide density.
side_a_arguments: Tree preservation, yard landscaping, and driveway rules already achieved by NPOs are being embedded universally into the new RD base districts.
NPO petitions currently lack a minimum neighbor-approval percentage (like 51% or 60%) and favor wealthier, better-organized neighborhoods while pushing growth onto less-organized communities.
Restricting height (such as 31 feet in Old West Durham) conflicts with the Comprehensive Plan's push for density and 15-minute walkable neighborhoods.
conflicts.side_b_position: Open to retaining an NPO-like mechanism or local petition tool as a release valve if capped by Comprehensive Plan guardrails.
side_b_arguments: Residents need a legislative release valve to protect neighborhoods with existing small homes from mass teardown and mansionization.
Overlay rules could be constrained by statute or local guardrails so they cannot undo Comprehensive Plan density goals.
conflicts.resolution: Planning Director Bo Dobrzenski and Director Young agreed to return with a staff analysis on standardizing beneficial NPO rules citywide and putting guardrails on NPOs and private text amendments.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - February 5, 2025
conflicts.issue: Draft New UDO Rural Density, Dimensional Standards & Anti-Displacement vs. Housing Supply Flexibility
conflicts.summary: Committee members debated how strictly the New UDO should constrain peripheral/PUD master-planned growth and tighten dimensional infill rules versus preserving flexibility for affordable housing under NC SB 382 constraints.
conflicts.side_a_position: Maintain tight controls against peripheral greenfield expansion and enforce strong dimensional/form-based protections in existing neighborhoods to curb teardowns and speculative gentrification.
side_a_arguments: Holding ~17,000 unincorporated acres inside the UGB at RB prevents premature suburban sprawl before infrastructure is ready.
Stronger dimensional rules and scrutiny of discretionary annexations/PUDs protect neighborhood character and natural open space.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid overly rigid dimensional barriers or removing master-planned/PUD flexibility in ways that hinder housing production and affordable developments while navigating SB 382.
side_b_arguments: Senate Bill 382 prohibits creating nonconformities or downzoning without owner consent, limiting what can be restricted directly by map rewrite.
Excessively tight infill rules or removing flexible master-planned pathways can unintentionally raise housing costs and restrict supply.
conflicts.resolution: Informational workshop; staff noted comments as Module 2 drafting and SB 382 legal analysis continue.

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) December 3, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) reviewed consolidated monthly development case summaries across the Urban Growth Boundary and held extensive work-session policy discussions on the draft New Unified Development Ordinance (UDO). Committee members debated the acreage threshold for Planned Development Districts, the sunset date for pre-2015 approved development plans, sidewalk requirements outside the Urban Growth Boundary, and the pace of the UDO adoption schedule versus Planning Commission review capacity. No substantive UDO policies came to a formal vote; the committee took two procedural voice votes approving the November 5, 2025 minutes and excusing absences including Council Member Matt Kopac.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Agenda Adjustments, and RTP 3.0 Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Jacobs opened the meeting while awaiting a quorum, which arrived at 00:05:42 with Vice Chair Nate Baker, Planning Commissioner Shagaris, and Commissioner Burton present (Javiera Caballero joined later at 00:29:42). Chair Jacobs announced that the Durham County Board of Commissioners had approved the RTP 3.0 rezoning prior to Thanksgiving following the county's earlier $20 million hub investment.

agenda_items.title: Approval of November 5, 2025 Meeting Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Once quorum was confirmed following roll call, the committee considered the November 5, 2025 JCCPC meeting minutes. Vice Chair Nate Baker moved approval and Commissioner Burton seconded with no edits requested.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Case Summaries
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented eight active zoning map change applications, predominantly small townhouse and multifamily residential projects inside the Urban Growth Boundary. Vice Chair Nate Baker highlighted positively that recent submittals have shifted away from large suburban subdivisions toward smaller infill projects within existing growth boundaries.

agenda_items.title: New UDO: Planned Development Districts and Pre-2015 Development Plan Sunsets
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff briefed JCCPC on mapping rules for existing approved development plans—proposing to revert pre-2015 unbuilt projects to standard UDO base districts—and proposed a 150-acre minimum threshold for Planned Development (PD) districts. Nate Baker urged lowering the PD minimum to 50–80 acres to allow coordinated master-planned infill, whereas Javiera Caballero cautioned that smaller PD sites struggle to finance public benefits such as schools and parks, and Chair Jacobs floated a compromise around 100 acres.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Commissioners Lee, Valentine, and Council Member Matt Kopac
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After Javiera Caballero arrived and joined the committee, members formally voted to excuse the absences of Commissioner Lee, Commissioner Valentine, and Council Member Matt Kopac.

agenda_items.title: New UDO Review Timeline, Planning Commission Schedule, and County Sidewalks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Members clashed over whether to expedite UDO adoption or preserve multi-meeting Planning Commission review, sparked by Javiera Caballero's critique of community engagement around the Northgate Mall site and Nate Baker's defense of deliberative Planning Commission review amid state downzoning restrictions. Staff also sought direction on sidewalk construction rules outside the Urban Growth Boundary—whether to build along frontage, require off-site extensions within a quarter-mile, or mandate sidewalk completion along adopted Bike+Walk and rail trail plans.

votes.notes: Javiera Caballero arrived later at 00:29:42; Matt Kopac, Commissioner Lee, and Commissioner Valentine were absent.

Nate Baker moved to approve the minutes and Commissioner Burton seconded the motion without objection or requested corrections. The motion carried unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Approval of Excused Absences for Commissioners Lee, Valentine, and Council Member Matt Kopac
votes.notes: Vote occurred following Javiera Caballero's arrival at 00:29:42.
votes.discussion_detail: Following Javiera Caballero's arrival during the New UDO presentation, Vice Chair Nate Baker requested a formal vote to record excused absences for absent committee members before continuing the technical UDO discussion. Committee members noted absences for county appointees Lee and Valentine alongside city appointee Matt Kopac, who was joining the seated council cohort starting in December 2025. Nate Baker moved to approve the excused absences and Javiera Caballero seconded. The committee approved the motion unanimously by voice vote.

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC)
meetings.executive_summary: At the November 2025 Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) meeting (referred to in the opening greeting as the November 5 meeting), city appointees Nate Baker and Javiera Caballero joined county appointees under Chair Jacobs, while Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton received an excused absence. Following unanimous procedural voice votes excusing Middleton and approving the October 1 minutes, Ted Halpern presented the Durham Housing Initiative Task Force Land Use Subcommittee Report, sparking a sustained policy clash between Javiera Caballero and Nate Baker over blanket by-right residential density bonuses versus discretionary review and anti-displacement safeguards. The committee then reviewed New UDO infill standards, compact RD2 zoning options, building heights, and the June 2026 UDO adoption schedule.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - August 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: New UDO Broad By-Right Upzoning vs. Preserving Base Zoning Leverage for Affordable Housing Density Bonuses
disagreements.summary: Committee members clashed over staff's draft UDO zoning capacity analysis, which increases by-right residential capacity inside the Urban Growth Boundary by 46% from 136,445 to 200,072 units.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold base by-right zoning closer to current capacity and tie significant additional height/density to calibrated affordable housing and green-building density bonuses.
side_a_arguments: Expanding by-right zoning to 200,072+ units gives away valuable development rights for free, especially under North Carolina's recent ban on local downzoning.
Without holding base zoning low enough to require developers to opt in, Durham loses leverage to extract affordable units and green building features via density bonuses.
Extra height (such as increasing 3-story corridors to 10-30 stories) should be unlocked through market-calibrated bonus tiers rather than unconditioned by-right entitlements.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain broad by-right residential upzoning inside the UGB to expand total housing supply, support walkable 15-minute neighborhoods, and rely on direct public subsidies for deep affordability.
side_b_arguments: Durham's existing 15% affordable housing density bonus has historically produced very few units because 0-30% AMI housing requires direct capital subsidies and revolving loan funds rather than zoning trades alone.
Restricting base supply risks Chapel Hill-style exclusionary outcomes—declining school enrollment, soaring home prices, and loss of Black residents.
Recent local market data (12% multifamily vacancy) indicates increased by-right supply helps moderate market rents while containing sprawl within the Urban Growth Boundary.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; committee directed Planning staff to return with data on historical density bonus uptake, Minneapolis inclusionary zoning comparisons, and visual scenario illustrations.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - April 2, 2025
disagreements.issue: Elimination of Minimum Parking Requirements in New UDO Module 2
disagreements.summary: Committee members differed over whether the new UDO should maintain complete elimination of off-street parking minimums in an auto-oriented city or monitor and revisit spillover impacts.
disagreements.side_a_position: Concerned about zero parking minimums causing street spillover and public/visitor parking burdens.
side_a_arguments: Durham remains heavily auto-dependent and visitors still drive to businesses and neighborhoods.
Without minimum parking requirements, private developments may shift parking costs and spillover burdens onto neighboring streets and the public.
disagreements.side_b_position: Strongly support permanently eliminating parking minimums to reduce housing/development costs and public parking debt.
side_b_arguments: Eliminating parking minimums was a hard-fought SCAD/UDO victory aligned with Durham's Comprehensive Plan.
Oversupplying parking created substantial debt and deficits in the City's downtown parking fund for underutilized garages.
disagreements.resolution: Staff confirmed there is no Council/County direction to restore parking minimums and that staff will monitor real-world impacts after adoption.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - April 2, 2025
disagreements.issue: Retaining Versus Eliminating Neighborhood Protection Overlays (NPOs) in New UDO
disagreements.summary: Members debated whether Neighborhood Protection Overlays reinforce inequitable density exclusion or can be reformed with guardrails to discourage small-home teardowns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Oppose retaining NPOs due to redundancy, lack of petition thresholds, and inequitable barriers to citywide density.
side_a_arguments: Tree preservation, yard landscaping, and driveway rules already achieved by NPOs are being embedded universally into the new RD base districts.
NPO petitions currently lack a minimum neighbor-approval percentage (like 51% or 60%) and favor wealthier, better-organized neighborhoods while pushing growth onto less-organized communities.
Restricting height (such as 31 feet in Old West Durham) conflicts with the Comprehensive Plan's push for density and 15-minute walkable neighborhoods.
disagreements.side_b_position: Open to retaining an NPO-like mechanism or local petition tool as a release valve if capped by Comprehensive Plan guardrails.
side_b_arguments: Residents need a legislative release valve to protect neighborhoods with existing small homes from mass teardown and mansionization.
Overlay rules could be constrained by statute or local guardrails so they cannot undo Comprehensive Plan density goals.
disagreements.resolution: Planning Director Bo Dobrzenski and Director Young agreed to return with a staff analysis on standardizing beneficial NPO rules citywide and putting guardrails on NPOs and private text amendments.

disagreements.issue: Draft New UDO Rural Density, Dimensional Standards & Anti-Displacement vs. Housing Supply Flexibility

disagreements.side_a_position: Maintain tight controls against peripheral greenfield expansion and enforce strong dimensional/form-based protections in existing neighborhoods to curb teardowns and speculative gentrification.

Stronger dimensional rules and scrutiny of discretionary annexations/PUDs protect neighborhood character and natural open space.

side_b_arguments: Senate Bill 382 prohibits creating nonconformities or downzoning without owner consent, limiting what can be restricted directly by map rewrite.
Excessively tight infill rules or removing flexible master-planned pathways can unintentionally raise housing costs and restrict supply.
disagreements.resolution: Informational workshop; staff noted comments as Module 2 drafting and SB 382 legal analysis continue.

disagreements.issue: Stormwater Exempt-Plat Rules Disincentivizing Triplexes & Quadplexes Under the New UDO
disagreements.summary: While not an explicit member-vs-member split, members and staff highlighted policy tension between UDO infill density goals and separate Public Works stormwater rules that exempt fee-simple single-family/duplex lots while penalizing missing-middle plexes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Coordinate Public Works and County Stormwater reforms alongside the UDO rewrite so compact multi-unit housing (triplexes/quadplexes) is not penalized relative to exempt-plat single-family infill.
side_a_arguments: Separate exempt-plat single-family driveways can generate more untreated impervious surface than a shared triplex/quadplex yet escape costly engineering analyses.
Without parallel stormwater reforms (such as footprint-based thresholds or Hillsboro-style topsoil/compost amendments), New UDO missing-middle zoning will fail to deliver diverse housing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Caution against altering stormwater thresholds without thorough engineering and state NPDES/EMC compliance review to avoid worsening downstream flooding.
side_b_arguments: Staff noted stormwater rules live outside the UDO and require technical capacity, state approvals, and careful maintenance oversight for green infrastructure like permeable pavement.
disagreements.resolution: Director Sara Young agreed to consult Public Works and County Stormwater leadership (Ryan Eaves) on feasible follow-up recommendations.
